entities.name: Andrew, Duke of Calabria
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Andrew, Duke of Calabria, born around 1327 and tragically deceased in 1345, was a pivotal, if ill-fated, figure in the complex Angevin dynastic struggles of 14th-century Southern Italy and Central Europe. As the son of Charles I of Hungary and brother of Louis I of Hungary, and the first husband of Joanna I of Naples, his brief life became a flashpoint for competing claims to the wealthy Kingdom of Naples. His marriage, intended to unite the Hungarian and Neapolitan branches of the Angevin dynasty, instead became the catalyst for one of the era's most notorious political assassinations, plunging the region into prolonged conflict.

Andrew arrived in Naples in 1334, at age seven, to marry his cousin Joanna, then eight, as stipulated by their grandfathers, Robert the Wise of Naples and Charles Martel of Anjou. The marriage, consummated in 1342, was fraught with tension due to Andrew's Hungarian entourage and the Neapolitan court's desire to limit his power. Despite a papal bull from Clement VI in 1344 granting him the right to be crowned King alongside Joanna, effectively making him co-ruler, the Neapolitan nobility, possibly including Joanna herself, resisted this elevation. His perceived arrogance and foreign influence further alienated the court, culminating in his brutal murder by strangulation at Aversa on September 18, 1345, while Joanna was pregnant with their son, Charles Martel.

The assassination of Andrew, Duke of Calabria, dramatically altered the political landscape of Southern Italy, triggering the Neapolitan War of Succession. His brother, Louis I of Hungary, vowed vengeance, launching two devastating invasions of Naples in 1347 and 1350, portraying himself as a crusader against regicides and infidels. This conflict not only destabilized the Kingdom of Naples for decades but also entangled the Papacy and various Italian city-states, significantly impacting the balance of power in the Mediterranean and diverting resources from other European conflicts.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Andrew's assassination directly ignited a brutal war between Hungary and Naples, destabilizing Southern Italy for decades and significantly impacting wider European diplomacy and the Papacy.
